newsitem.title: JAPAN: Tokyo forex trading hit 6-year volume high in '96.
newsitem.headline: Tokyo forex trading hit 6-year volume high in '96.

text.p: Tokyo foreign exchange trading volume surged to a six-year high in 1996, raising hopes among dealers that the long-suffering market may at last be poised for a lasting recovery.

"It is becoming a more active market, and there will be no change in that this year. Spot (dollar/yen trade) has definitely come off the bottom," said Kazuo Fujii, president of Nittan Exco, one of Japan's largest currency brokers.
"I think we'll see a similar (volume) picture in 1997, if not higher," said Chris Pavlou, treasurer at Midland Bank Plc.

But others weren't convinced the market was out of the woods, citing Japan's slow economic recovery and restructuring in foreign banks, which is causing some operators to pull out of the Tokyo market.

"I'm not too sure it shows real recovery... The market trend was not very clear and just moved back and forth a lot, which may have caused volume to pick up superficially," said Takao Sakoh, first vice-president at Union Bank of Switzerland.

According to figures compiled by Japan's Ministry of Finance (MOF), the volume of dollar-for-yen swap and spot transactions through brokers rose to nearly $5.27 trillion in 1996, the most since an all-time record of $5.96 trillion in 1990.

Dealers cited a number of factors behind the gains, including trading in an increasingly diverse number of currencies and a shift to earlier release times for economic indicators that allowed the Tokyo market to respond over most of a trading day.

But the largest factor was a massive wave of foreign investment by both institutional and individual investors drawn by historically low Japanese interest rates -- a trend that dealers expect to continue.
Sidney Hui, vice-president at Bank of America in Tokyo, said he expects investors to remain in the market.

But others said the pace of investment could start to slow. "Yields (in Australia) have been steadily decreasing, and this may make investments here less attractive," a dealer with an Australian bank in Tokyo said.

But others, including Midland's Pavlou, said investors were likely to merely shift assets to other foreign instruments, especially those denominated in sterling, which gained sharply against the yen in 1996. Increasingly active trade in sterling also played a role in higher Tokyo volume, he added.
One peculiarity of 1996 was an extremely narrow trading range, which saw the greenback move between 103.97 and 116.18 yen.

Although some were frustrated by the lack of volatility, which kept interest rate spreads narrow and reduced activity in longer-term swap trades, the lack of extreme moves also gave many investors the confidence to venture overseas.

"In 1996, Japanese investors became more willing to take risks, particularly on longer-term overseas instruments, because they now feel secure that wild swings in the dollar are unlikely. And they're no longer willing to wait for higher Japanese rates," Nittan's Fujii said.

But all is not rosy. Many remain concerned about Tokyo stocks, whose main share index plunged more than 10 percent in the first trading week of 1997, although it recovered slightly last week. Renewed losses are seen inhibiting potential foreign investment.

And while the forex market is scheduled for some deregulation in 1998, many in the market feel that even more sweeping changes may be needed, and sooner than the 2001 called for by Prime Minister Ryutaro Hashimoto.
"If the government would move a bit faster towards a freer market, the market will become even more optimistic," Nittan's Fujii said.
